meta.title: Who really said "If I were your wife I'd put poison in your tea! If I were your husband I'd drink it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lloyd George and not Churchill: the poison-in-your-tea joke descends from an anonymous newspaper filler of 18 November 1899.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I were your wife I'd put poison in your tea! If I were your husband I'd drink it'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1899 newspaper gag, pinned on Lloyd George in 1932 and on Churchill and Nancy Astor by 1952. Quote Investigator traced the trail.

answer.label: Not David Lloyd George — an anonymous 1899 newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: Credited to David Lloyd George (1863–1945), British Prime Minister 1916–1922 — but only from 1932
answer.sourceLine: The exchange was already circulating as an unsigned newspaper gag in November 1899, with two anonymous strangers on a streetcar and no famous names attached. The earliest telling that puts it in Lloyd George’s mouth is a 1932 Montreal newspaper column on public speaking; the far more famous Churchill and Nancy Astor version appears only from 1949 onward. No contemporary record of Lloyd George saying it has ever been produced.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — a stock heckler joke that was in print thirty-two years before anyone credited it to Lloyd George.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: 18 November 1899, page 2 — anonymous, credited to the “Listener”
Oswego Daily Times, Oswego, New York
The Montreal Gazette, 4 January 1932 — “Art of Public Speech” by Rev. R. G. Burgoyne
The New York Times, 6 February 1949; Nancy Astor added in The Glitter and the Gold (1952)

source.excerpt: The “Listener” reports the following from the subway: On one of the recent warm days a sour-visaged, fussy lady got on one of the smoking seats on an open car in the subway. Next her sat a man who was smoking a cigar… The lady fussed and wriggled, and grew angrier, and looked at the man scornfully. Presently she could endure it no longer. She looked squarely at him and said: “If you were my husband, sir, I’d give you a dose of poison!” The man looked at her. “If I were your husband,” said he, “I’d take it!”
trail: November 1899 — nobody famous. The earliest known printing is an unsigned filler in the Oswego Daily Times of 18 November 1899, credited to the “Listener”; the researcher Barry Popik identified it, and Quote Investigator laid out the whole trail ↗. A version with a drunk passenger ran in The Chicago Tribune on 3 January 1900.

February 1921 — a by-election candidate, not a Prime Minister. A report headed ‘A Candidate’s Retort’ in the Yorkshire Evening Post of 24 February 1921 has a woman heckler tell Llewelyn Williams she would put poison in his tea, and Williams answer that he would drink it — the modern wording, in Britain, before either statesman was credited with it, per Beachcombing’s survey of the joke ↗.

January 1932 — Lloyd George gets the credit. The single Lloyd George citation documented by QI ↗ is a Montreal Gazette article on the art of public speech, in which a heckler offers him poison and he replies that he would take it quickly. It is an illustration in a rhetoric column, not a report of an occasion.

1949 to 1952 — it becomes Churchill and Astor, and stays there. After The New York Times and Consuelo Vanderbilt Balsan, the exchange became Churchill’s. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, and Professor Buzzkill returns a verdict of No Quote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Note what is missing in 1899: no tea, no coffee, no politician, no Lady Astor. Two strangers on a streetcar, and a punchline of “I’d take it” rather than “I’d drink it.” The drink, the platform heckle and the famous names were all added later.

source.rightsNote: The joke has no identifiable author. Its early printings — the Oswego Daily Times item of 18 November 1899 and the newspaper and stage versions that followed through the 1920s — are anonymous and long out of copyright, but there is no single authored work to which this wording can be attached. The celebrity form most people quote today descends from Consuelo Vanderbilt Balsan’s The Glitter and the Gold (1952), which remains in copyright, so quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for the popular wording.

author.name: David Lloyd George
author.heading: About David Lloyd George
author.metaLine: 1863–1945 · Welsh Liberal statesman; British Prime Minister, 1916–1922
author.bio: Lloyd George sat for Caernarvon Boroughs from 1890, served as Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1908 to 1915 — the People’s Budget of 1909 was his — and was Prime Minister from 1916 to 1922. He was Welsh-speaking, raised in Llanystumdwy, and had a reputation as a formidable platform speaker in an era when heckling was part of the job, which is exactly the sort of reputation that attracts other people’s jokes. This one is not his: the poison retort appears nowhere in the sourced sections of his Wikiquote page ↗, in its Misattributed section or anywhere else.

cite.sourceCitation: “Right and Left” (untitled short item), Oswego Daily Times (Oswego, New York), 18 November 1899, page 2, column 4 — anonymous, credited to the “Listener.” Identified by researcher Barry Popik and documented in Garson O’Toole, “Anecdote Origin: ‘If I Were Your Wife I’d Put Poison in Your Tea!’ ‘If I Were Your Husband I’d Drink It,’” Quote Investigator, 27 August 2014. The Lloyd George telling is first documented in The Montreal Gazette, 4 January 1932. Attribution to Lloyd George unverified.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been given this line
misattribution.intro: This is a joke rather than a quotation, and it has been handed from one famous name to the next for well over a century. Each retelling swaps the drink, the insult and the speakers. None of them is the origin.

items.why: The only Lloyd George telling documented by Quote Investigator ↗ is an article on public speaking by Rev. R. G. Burgoyne in The Montreal Gazette of 4 January 1932 — more than thirty years after the joke first reached print, and with a different punchline: the heckler says she would give him poison, and he replies that he would take it quickly. Nothing places the line with him at the time.

The New York Times gave the retort to Churchill and an unnamed politically minded lady on 6 February 1949; Nancy Astor was written in by Consuelo Vanderbilt Balsan in The Glitter and the Gold (1952), with coffee instead of tea. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed ↗, and the International Churchill Society calls it incorrectly attributed ↗, suggesting F. E. Smith as a likelier speaker.

Groucho Marx put the punchline in Shaw’s mouth in a 1962 newspaper column, then noted in the same breath that it had already been credited to a whole gaggle of wags, an American League umpire among them — column reproduced by QI ↗.

The American humorist told the Cleveland Plain Dealer in March 1900 that he had invented the gag himself and that it had already worn out from travelling. But it was in newspapers the previous November, and QI calls his claim fascinating but uncertain ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest known version, printed in the Oswego Daily Times on 18 November 1899, has no famous names in it at all — two strangers on a streetcar, a cigar, and a dose of poison. Everything after that is a joke in search of a celebrity: Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this joke keeps changing owners
lead: It is not really a quotation at all; it is a two-line vaudeville routine, and it has spent more than a century looking for a celebrity to attach itself to. In 1899 the participants are two strangers on a streetcar. In 1900 the American humorist Marshall Pinckney Wilder claims he invented it the other week. In 1902 a Broadway play swaps the sexes. Only in the 1930s does it start landing on statesmen, and by the 1950s it has settled on Winston Churchill and Nancy Astor — the pattern Nigel Rees named Churchillian Drift ↗, in which a good line drifts from an obscure speaker to a famous one.

The Lloyd George version is a stop along that route rather than the origin. That the joke was ordinary campaign-trail currency in his own political world is easy to show: the Yorkshire Evening Post of 24 February 1921 ran a short item headed ‘A Candidate’s Retort’ in which a woman heckler tells the by-election candidate Llewelyn Williams she would put poison in his tea, and he answers that he would drink it — the modern wording, in a British newspaper, years before either Lloyd George or Churchill was credited with it. Beachcombing’s history of the joke ↗ collected that citation.
detailsBody: September 1902 — the roles reverse. The New York Times collected laugh lines from new New York productions and picked this out of “Captain Molly”: the man offers the poison and the woman says she would take it, per Quote Investigator ↗.

June 1913 — a man is hospitalised by it. The Milwaukee Sentinel reported that Julius Jeswein, having heard what it called a veteran vaudeville joke, laughed for sixteen consecutive hours, stopped the act, and had to be sedated at the Emergency hospital. The paper’s own view of the gag was that nobody should find it funny for three seconds — reproduced by QI ↗.

1935 and 1962 — screen and column. Patricia Ellis and Joe E. Brown trade the lines in the Warner Bros. film “Bright Lights”, and in 1962 Groucho Marx retold it in his newspaper column with George Bernard Shaw as the wit, adding that it had already been credited to “a whole gaggle of wags” — both citations at QI ↗.
context.pull: In 1899 it is two strangers on a streetcar. The famous names arrive half a century later.

schema.verdictNote: Not a quotation but an anonymous joke, commonly misattributed to David Lloyd George and later to Winston Churchill and Nancy Astor. The earliest known printing — an unsigned filler in the Oswego Daily Times of 18 November 1899 — is worded differently ('I'd give you a dose of poison' / 'I'd take it'); this tea-and-drink-it form is not documented until the Yorkshire Evening Post of 24 February 1921. The true author is not established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest known instance is an anonymous item in the Oswego Daily Times of 18 November 1899 (credited to the 'Listener', identified by Barry Popik); a drunk-passenger version ran in The Chicago Tribune 3 January 1900; Marshall Pinckney Wilder claimed authorship in the Cleveland Plain Dealer, March 1900; the Lloyd George anecdote appears in The Montreal Gazette of 4 January 1932 in 'Art of Public Speech' by Rev. R. G. Burgoyne with the punchline 'Madam, if I were your husband I'd take it quickly'; The New York Times of 6 February 1949 gave it to Churchill; Consuelo Vanderbilt Balsan's The Glitter and the Gold (1952) added Nancy Astor and coffee; Groucho Marx credited Shaw in 1962; QI concludes the earliest participants were anonymous and the Churchill evidence is not persuasive.

Wikiquote's Winston Churchill page lists the Lady Nancy Astor 'poison in your coffee' exchange in its Misattributed section, noting it dates to 1899, is of American humour origin, that coffee was added in 1900, and that it was incorrectly attributed in Consuelo Vanderbilt Balsan's Glitter and Gold (1952).

Wikiquote's David Lloyd George page contains no poison-in-your-tea or poison-in-your-coffee retort in any section, including its Misattributed section (which lists only a remark about Mustafa Kemal Ataturk).

Professor Buzzkill returns a verdict of 'No Quote' on the Churchill poisoned-tea exchange, states there is no solid evidence he said it, and credits Garson O'Toole of Quote Investigator with tracing it to the 'Listener' section of The Oswego Daily Times of 18 November 1899.

The blog quotes a Yorkshire Evening Post item of 24 February 1921, page 6, headed 'A Candidate's Retort': a heckler says 'If I were your wife I would put poison in your tea' and Mr Llewelyn Williams replies 'And if I were your husband I would drink it'.

The International Churchill Society lists the Nancy Astor poison exchange among incorrectly attributed quotes and says it is much more likely that Churchill's friend Lord Birkenhead (F. E. Smith) said it.

Wikipedia defines Churchillian Drift as the widespread misattribution of quotes by obscure figures to more famous figures, credits Nigel Rees with the term, and includes the Astor poison-in-the-coffee exchange as an example that dates to 1899.

David Lloyd George was born 17 January 1863 and died 26 March 1945; he was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom 1916-1922, Chancellor of the Exchequer 1908-1915 (the 1909 People's Budget), MP for Caernarvon Boroughs from an 1890 by-election, and was raised in Llanystumdwy with Welsh as his first language.
